title: WhatsApp Business Message Templates: Rules, Categories, Examples, and Approval Basics
description: Understand WhatsApp business message templates, categories, components, approval basics, examples, and team workflows for safer customer messaging.
excerpt: A practical guide to WhatsApp business message templates: when they are needed, how categories work, what components to use, and how teams can manage approvals.
author: TalkWagon Editorial Team
heroImageAlt: TalkWagon template management dashboard showing WhatsApp business message template categories, approval workflow, languages, and preview cards

faqs.question: What is a WhatsApp business message template?
faqs.answer: A WhatsApp business message template is a pre-approved message format used by a business to start or continue certain WhatsApp conversations at scale, especially outside the customer service window on the WhatsApp Business Platform.

faqs.question: Which WhatsApp template categories are commonly used?
faqs.answer: Meta categorizes templates into marketing, utility, and authentication use cases. The correct category depends on the message purpose, not just the wording.

faqs.question: What parts can a WhatsApp message template include?
faqs.answer: Templates can include components such as a header, body, footer, and buttons. The body carries the main text and variables, while buttons can support replies, links, or actions.

faqs.question: Why do WhatsApp templates get rejected?
faqs.answer: Common reasons include unclear purpose, incorrect category, misleading content, poor variable context, policy-sensitive wording, missing opt-out handling for marketing messages, or text that does not match the selected use case.

faqs.question: Can quick replies replace WhatsApp templates?
faqs.answer: No. Quick replies help agents answer faster inside conversations. Templates are approved message assets used for business-initiated or structured messaging workflows. They solve different problems.

faqs.question: How should teams manage templates?
faqs.answer: Teams should keep a template library with owners, categories, languages, approval status, variable rules, use cases, review dates, and performance notes so campaigns and service messages are not sent with outdated or risky content.
